channel.title: The Officer's Bookshelf
channel.description: Long-form conversations about books worth reading closely. Each week takes on a single title — an overview first, then chapter by chapter, then the themes still worth arguing about long after the last page.

item.title: E7 · Closing Review — Conflict
item.description: A closing conversation on Conflict as a whole: what Petraeus and Roberts argue about strategic leadership across eight decades of war, whether their four tasks of the strategic leader hold up as a lens on the record, and where the book's judgments are most and least persuasive.
item.content:encoded:
A closing conversation on Conflict: The Evolution of Warfare from 1945 to Ukraine as a whole. We pull the threads together: the authors' recurring argument that outcomes turn on strategic leadership — getting the big ideas right, communicating them, overseeing their execution, and refining them as the fight changes.

We weigh what the book gets right and where it strains: how much Petraeus's own experience shapes the verdicts, whether the "great captain" framing does justice to the role of institutions and luck, and what their reading of the record implies for the wars still to come.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E6 · Part 5: Ukraine & the Future of War — Conflict
item.description: The final part: Russia's 2014 seizure of Crimea and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the authors' conclusions on where warfare is heading — drones, precision, cyber and space, artificial intelligence, and what stays constant even as the character of war keeps changing.
item.content:encoded:
The final part of Conflict: Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea and war in the Donbas, and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 — why Moscow's assumptions failed, how Ukraine's defense held, and what the war has revealed about drones, precision strike, and the transparency of the modern battlefield.

From there Petraeus and Roberts turn to the future: the pull of unmanned systems, cyber and space, and artificial intelligence, set against their insistence that the nature of war endures even as its character is transformed.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E5 · Part 4: Afghanistan & Iraq — Conflict
item.description: The post-9/11 wars: the intervention in Afghanistan, the 2003 invasion of Iraq and the insurgency that followed, and the counterinsurgency campaign and surge — the stretch of the book closest to Petraeus's own command experience.
item.content:encoded:
The post-9/11 wars in Conflict: the toppling of the Taliban in Afghanistan, the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and the descent into insurgency and sectarian violence that the initial plans had not reckoned with.

This is the ground Petraeus knows firsthand, and the account leans into it: the rewriting of counterinsurgency doctrine, the 2007 surge in Iraq, and the hard argument over how much difference command and strategy made — set beside the long, unresolved war in Afghanistan.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E4 · Part 3: Cold War's End & the New Disorder — Conflict
item.description: The late Cold War and its aftermath: the Soviet quagmire in Afghanistan, the Falklands, the decisive First Gulf War of 1991, and the wars of the 1990s that broke out as the bipolar order fell away.
item.content:encoded:
The turn from the Cold War to what came after, as told in Conflict: the Soviet Union's own draining war in Afghanistan, Britain's campaign in the Falklands, and the 1991 Gulf War — a swift, overwhelming coalition victory that seemed, at the time, to promise a new model of decisive conventional war.

Then the disorder that followed the Soviet collapse: the Balkans and the other conflicts of the 1990s, where the clean lessons of 1991 proved far harder to apply.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E3 · Part 2: Vietnam & Cold War Hot Wars — Conflict
item.description: The wars at the Cold War's height: Vietnam in depth — escalation, attrition, and the limits of American strategy — alongside the Arab–Israeli wars and the other "hot" conflicts fought under the shadow of superpower rivalry.
item.content:encoded:
The middle of the Cold War, as Conflict tells it, centered on Vietnam: the escalation of American involvement, the strategy of attrition and its failure, and the gap between battlefield performance and political outcome that defined the war.

Around it, the other hot wars of the era — the Arab–Israeli wars of 1967 and 1973 chief among them — and what they revealed about armor, air power, surprise, and the strategic leadership that turned tactical results into lasting effect, or squandered them.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E2 · Part 1: Postwar & Decolonization — Conflict
item.description: The first stretch after 1945: the Chinese Civil War, Korea, and the long wars of decolonization — Indochina and Dien Bien Phu, Malaya, Algeria — where great powers learned, often painfully, how irregular war and national liberation would reshape conflict.
item.content:encoded:
The opening period of Conflict, from 1945 into the 1960s: the communist victory in the Chinese Civil War, the war in Korea and its costly stalemate, and the wars of decolonization that pulled the European empires apart.

Indochina and the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, the British campaign in Malaya, and the Algerian war become the authors' first case studies in irregular warfare — where conventional strength ran up against insurgency, politics, and the will of populations.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E1 · Overview — Conflict
item.description: General David Petraeus and historian Andrew Roberts survey the evolution of warfare from 1945 to Ukraine, arguing that the thread running through eight decades of conflict is strategic leadership. A full-book overview of their central argument and the sweep of wars the book covers, before the part-by-part episodes that follow.
item.content:encoded:
Conflict: The Evolution of Warfare from 1945 to Ukraine (2023) pairs General David Petraeus, who commanded in Iraq and Afghanistan, with the historian Andrew Roberts for a survey of eight decades of war — from the wars of decolonization to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

This first episode takes the book whole: the authors' central claim that strategic leadership is the thread tying these conflicts together — the leader's task of getting the big ideas right, communicating them, driving their execution, and refining them — and how that lens sets up the wars examined in the rest of the run.

The episodes that follow move through the book part by part: postwar and decolonization, Vietnam and the Cold War's hot wars, the Cold War's end and the new disorder, Afghanistan and Iraq, and Ukraine and the future of war — closing with a full-book review.
